newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-BECKHAM THE NATURAL HEIR TO CHARLTON'S THRONE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BECKHAM THE NATURAL HEIR TO CHARLTON'S THRONE.

text.p: Some soccer stars are spectacular goal-scorers, delivering their product in twos and threes and with metronomic regularity.
Others are the scorers of spectacular goals, playmakers or creators with a gift for supplying the flourish that burns an image on the memory.
Manchester United's David Beckham, dubbed by many as the natural heir to Bobby Charlton for both club and country, belongs, without doubt, in the second category.

On the opening day of the season, the flaxen-haired midfielder scored for United with a wonderful long-range lob, from inside his own half, against Wimbledon. It was outrageous and insprirational and bucked the trend for well-coached teamwork.
It was a goal too that alerted the British media to his rare and precocious talent and transformed his image from popular prodigy to proven product. Beckham, at only 21, had arrived.

Blessed with a powerful shot, an unerring eye for defence-splitting passes and goalscoring opportunities, the ability to pass long and short with equal accuracy and enough skill to mesmerise defenders and spectators, Beckham had suddenly arrived.

Several more dazzling goals, most recently two in successive weeks against Tottenham -- both struck with venom and precision from outside the penalty area -- have confirmed the feeling that the laconic Londoner is set for another successful year as the best young playmaker in the country.

Tottenham, knocked out of the FA Cup by Beckham's free-kick winner at Old Trafford and stunned by his even more glorious shot at White Hart Lane a week later, have more cause than most clubs to rue Beckham's ability.

His goals inflicted severe dents on their season and reminded them too that, but for a childhood dream, he could have been playing for them and not for United where he has graduated from a youth team which included Gary and Phil Neville, both now capped by England, Paul Scholes and Nicky butt.

For Beckham was not born in Manchester or northern England, but in north-east London not far from White Hart Lane on May 2, 1975. He was well-known as one of the best schoolboy prospects in the capital before leaving to play for his favourite club -- Manchester United.

At the time, he was training for one day each week with Spurs and their great north London rivals Arsenal. But, when the decision had to be made, he left instead for a new career in the footsteps of Charlton, United and England's most illustrious hard-shooting midfield player of the past.

"I always wanted to play for Manchester United because I had supported them since I was young," he explained, adding that suggestions that he was ignored by Spurs' then manager Terry Venables were not entirely accurate. Since those days, of course, Beckham has become a regular part of the England squad and Venables has been followed as England coach by Glenn Hoddle, who was one of Beckham's heroes as a boy.

Even for someone as extravagantly gifted as Beckham his progress has been meteoric. He did not make his full league debut for United until April 1995, but by the end of this season could find himself established in the England team and part of United's first European Cup-winning side since the Charlton-inspired side of 1968.

If that dream is realised, a Champions' Cup medal would sit very nicely alongside the domestic league and Cup medals Beckham collected last season, his first in the team. It is a prospect that dwarfs his pre-season ambitions.

"At the start of this season, my ambition was just to play as many first team games for Manchester United as possible," he told Total Football magazine. "There are a lot of brilliant players in our squad and I honestly had no targets beyond that. Getting into the England set-up has been absolutely unbelievable."

Modest and articulate, Beckham has managed to combine the eloquence of both Charlton and Hoddle on and off the pitch, aided by a sensible protection policy from Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson who chided him, tongue-in-cheek, for his selfish flash of imagination in the goal against Wimbledon by requesting that he does not attempt to repeat it each week.

Ferguson has prevented Beckham also from being exposed to media pressure, shielded him from reporters as much as possible, and also rested him from the first team to keep him fresh and help him avoid burning out early in his career. The occasional flash of ill-temper and bizzare incident in which he bared his buttocks incident at Southampton may have warned Ferguson of his latest prodigy's potential problems with over-exposure.
Beckham, however, is not frightened by the prospect of the kind of fame that is sure to come his way as he plays alongside Giggs and Frenchman Eric Cantona..
"It can be hard, but it's exciting too," he explained. "I don't take anything for granted, though. Things can change so quickly."

Then, in a comment which proved he does keep his feet firmly on the ground thanks to his family's solid London support for his career in the north, he added: "I don't believe I will ever get carried away because there are too many people who would knock me down.
"As well as all those at Old Trafford, I would have my father to answer to -- it won't happen."
